blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Explain why earnings differ between occupations, read the pattern in earnings figures, and describe in words the market forces behind a difference in pay.

blocks.heading: The reasons behind a pay gap
blocks.text: Earnings - the pay a worker receives over a period, including overtime and bonuses - differ because occupations differ. Skill and qualifications: a chartered accountant's work demands years of study. Scarcity: where few people hold what employers need, pay rises. Experience and responsibility: a mine shift supervisor answers for others and earns more than a new hire. Risk and conditions: a long-haul driver earns more than a pump attendant with a similar training period, because the job takes the driver from home for days at a stretch and employers must pay enough to keep people in it. Productivity and the balance of demand and supply in the occupation set the rest, and where a small number of large employers fix pay scales, their scales hold earnings down.

blocks.heading: Reading the gaps
blocks.text: A 2026 survey of average monthly earnings in Namibia found a petrol-station attendant on N$4 800, a school teacher with ten years in the job on N$14 200, and a chartered accountant on N$38 000. The accountant earns N$38 000 - N$4 800 = N$33 200 more than the attendant. Qualifying takes years of study and fees, few complete it, and employers compete for those who do. The teacher also holds a degree, yet many qualified teachers apply for posts against pay scales set by a small number of large employers, so the scarcity premium is missing. In Brazil, certified welders in the Rio Grande shipyards earn well above general welders for the same reason: certification is scarce, and the yards bid for it.

blocks.heading: The forces behind a difference, drawn in words
blocks.text: Picture the market for certified water engineers. The vertical axis measures the monthly wage in N$; the horizontal axis measures the number of certified engineers. At a low wage few engineers offer their services and employers seek many, so the number sought exceeds the number offered; at a high wage the reverse holds. The two lines cross at the wage where the numbers match. When new water-treatment projects raise the demand for engineers, the demand line moves outward: at the old wage employers now seek more engineers than the region holds, so the wage is bid up until the numbers match again at a higher wage, with more engineers at work. Over the years that follow, the higher wage draws students into training, the supply line moves outward too, and the premium narrows - provided employers' demand has stopped growing faster than the new supply.

blocks.heading: Bargaining strength, discrimination and government policy
blocks.text: Three further forces open or close earnings gaps between groups of workers. Bargaining strength: workers in a strong trade union, such as many mine workers, tend to earn more than similar workers with no union, because the employer must bargain with the whole workforce at once; shop assistants spread across many small businesses have little such power. Discrimination: treating workers differently in pay, hiring, training or promotion for reasons unrelated to their productivity - their gender, race or age, for example. A group discriminated against earns less, both because it may be paid less for the same work and because it is kept out of better-paid posts, so its members crowd into the jobs left open to them, where the extra supply holds pay down. Government policy: a minimum wage set above the market wage lifts the lowest earnings and so narrows the gap between the lowest-paid and the rest; equal-pay laws aim to remove gaps that rest on discrimination; and the pay scales the government sets for its own staff decide earnings across the public sector.

blocks.heading: Comparing groups of workers
blocks.text: Skilled and unskilled: skilled workers tend to earn more because their skills take time and money to acquire, so they are scarce relative to demand, and their output per hour is higher; many people can do unskilled work, so its supply is plentiful and its pay low. Primary, secondary and tertiary: the sector label does not set pay; the skill and productivity within each industry do. A farm labourer in the primary sector tends to earn little, because many unskilled workers compete for the work and output per worker is low, while a skilled mine worker in the same sector earns several times as much operating costly machinery in a demanding job. The tertiary sector runs from low-paid shop work to highly paid banking. Male and female: on average women tend to earn less than men, because more women work in lower-paid occupations or part-time, career breaks to care for children cut experience and promotion, and some employers discriminate. Private and public sectors: public-sector pay follows government pay scales limited by the budget and tends to come with greater job security and a pension, while private-sector pay follows each firm's demand for labour and its profits. A highly skilled accountant tends to earn more at a private bank; a cleaner or clerk may earn more, and with more security, in a ministry.

blocks.heading: More trainees, drawn in words
blocks.text: A change in supply is drawn the same way. Take the market for qualified welders in Walvis Bay. Put the monthly wage in N$ on the vertical axis and the number of welders on the horizontal axis; draw demand D sloping down and supply S1 sloping up, crossing at wage W1 with Q1 welders employed. A new training centre adds 150 qualified welders a year, so the supply curve shifts to the right, to S2. At the old wage W1 more welders now offer themselves than employers seek, so the wage is bid down. The new equilibrium is where D crosses S2: a lower wage, W2, and more welders employed, Q2. In words, the diagram shows that a larger pool of trained workers tends to lower the wage in that occupation while raising employment, unless demand for welders rises at the same time.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The scarcity that lifts some earnings begins in the training choices of this topic; the demand behind a rising wage traces back to product demand in topic 2.3; the employers doing the bidding are the firms of topic 3.5; and persistent pay gaps are one focus of the government's role in topic 4.1.
